-properties-plus-methods shape maps closely onto what a ViewModel already looks like.
The
object manages your application state, or a portion (scope) of it.
It is a class object with the following components:
A
type (typically an enum), which defines the events that occur within your application’s scope.
Member variables that represent the state of the application/scope. These variables should never be modified directly. Instead, the view or other components should send a
event to the scope, and the scope’s
method will handle state changes.
A public
method that forwards events for scope processing.
An internal
method that processes the current state and incoming
event, applying the business logic to produce a new state.
The
events are processed synchronously, meaning the state is updated immediately after sending an event. Asynchronous tasks, called
Effects
, are triggered as side effects. Each effect has a corresponding completion
event. Thus, a typical asynchronous task introduces two
events: one to start the effect and one to handle its completion.
The
object is intentionally designed as a class to manage the lifecycle of ongoing effects. When a
instance is released, all associated effects are canceled. This ensures that the lifespan of the object defines the lifespan of the effects.
For asynchronous tasks, the Statoscope object provides:
An
method to trigger asynchronous tasks during state updates.
, the list of ongoing effects.
Automatic cancellation of effects upon releasing the scope.
to cancel specific ongoing effects.

Defining a scope means defining at least the State of your application and the When events that may affect it. Some scopes don’t have asynchronous effects, so we will discuss Effects later. See it all together in a simple Statoscope:

inlineContent.text: State

is expressed with member variables, as usually done in other SwiftUI design patterns that use ObservableObject. This is an important design decision to make the transition to Statoscope smoother from other development patterns.
When
type enumerates the events that may take place in your app/screen.
There will usually be 3 big groups of the when cases. See how we intentionally selected a “sentence” format for our cases so it will help you describing the app behavior:
User driven actions: userTappedIncrementButton, userDismissedAlert…
System: systemLoadedTheScreen, systemMovedAppToBackground…
Effects feedback: next topic is all about effects… will get there soon

At the core design principle of the library we’ve added the testability principle, and we want to introduce it as soon as possible. When using sentence-like typing of the State and When events, the fact that the whens are an enum, and using some testing sugar helpers included in the library, testing looks as straightforward as this:
These test description accomplishes several things:
Describes the behavior of the application: accomplishing ACCEPTANCE AS CODE
Provides an out-of-the-box testing coverage
Documents common and supported scenarios. See it further in the testing section and using FORK

Side effects of our source code are events that may result in later state changes. These Effects are important to the Statoscope architecture. To keep using the pattern used until now (State[N] + Event[N] = State[N+1]), we will split an asynchronous task as 2 different When cases: the one that starts the asynchronous task, and the one receiving of the asynchronous result.

Now you can test not only state changes but also effects triggering. Please note Effects in a test environment are not executed, they’re just added to an enqueued list to check correct enqueueing, but never executed. Subsequent WHEN execution will clean up the queue. See how to test our example:

content.text: App state as Statoscope composition: Superscope + Subscope

inlineContent.text: A single
handling an entire screen tends to grow into a “god object”: feature toggles, list state, detail state, favorites — all mixed into one
enum and one
switch. Statoscope lets you split that into a tree of smaller scopes instead, connected with two property wrappers.
declares that a scope owns a child scope:

code: readingArticle = NewsFeedArticle(articleId: id)   // creates and wires the child scope

inlineContent.text: Assigning to
creates the child scope and links it into the injection tree; assigning
releases it. The parent can read and observe the live child directly through the property.
is the child’s side of the same relationship — a weak, read-only link back up to an ancestor scope, resolved through the injection tree rather than passed in by hand:

code: // read shared state from the parent without the parent handing it down explicitly

inlineContent.text: walks up the injection tree to find the nearest ancestor of the declared type — the same tree
dependency resolution uses (see Dependency Injection below), just resolving to a live scope instead of a plain value.
Splitting scopes this way keeps each
focused on one concern, makes each scope independently testable via
, and lets SwiftUI views compose the same way the scopes do — one view per scope, each observing only the state it owns. The tradeoff: state that’s genuinely shared across siblings (like
above) has to flow through
or dependency injection rather than living in one convenient place — usually a worthwhile trade once a screen has grown past two or three concerns, not something to reach for on day one.
only move data in one direction each: a parent hands a value down when it creates a child, and a child gets a read-only link back up. Neither lets a child’s
event
change what a parent owns.
is for that: a parent intercepts an event from a child before deciding whether to let it through.
Say favoriting an article needs to update a single, shared list of favorites — not a copy living separately in both
and
. Move ownership to the parent and let it intercept the child’s event:

inlineContent.text: Unlike the Reducer pattern’s

the parent’s own
processes,

directly, no delegation required. And where the Reducer pattern’s
fixes the ordering by construction (forwarding always happens first, unconditionally — there’s no way to intercept or veto it, and none is needed),
here is a call you make yourself: call it first to react
after
the child processes the event, last to react
before

That flexibility doesn’t remove the ordering pitfall, though — it just moves the decision point. A real app on the Reducer side of this same library reacted to a child’s submit event, and a guard inside the child’s own handler for that
same
event read a parent-owned flag the reaction had already flipped moments earlier, rejecting every legitimate submit. The
equivalent is exactly as possible: react-then-forward means the child’s own
for that event runs
after
your reaction already changed the state it might be checking.
One more contrast worth calling out: a child can point
past its direct parent, straight at any ancestor by type (
walks the whole chain the same way, so an ancestor two levels up intercepts a grandchild’s event with no relay code in the reducer in between). For the Reducer pattern’s
, that skip-level read is only safe when the data lives directly on the target ancestor’s own state — a value snapshot mirroring some
other
descendant’s data can go stale.
has no such trap: it resolves to a
live reference
to the actual ancestor object, not a value copied at some point in time, so skipping levels is always safe here — there’s nothing cached in between to go stale.

abstract.text: Explore the core concepts of the Statostore pattern through examples.
A lightweight library for managing state in iOS applications, designed with simplicity, testability, and scalability in mind.
Statoscope is a small library to build apps with state management,
testing, effects management and dependency injection.
Explore the core concepts of the Statoscope architecture through examples.
